reference.source: Textbook of Autoinflammation / Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology
clinicalPearls: An adult-onset periodic fever syndrome associated with specific NOD2 gene variants, distinct from Blau syndrome and Crohn disease
Presents with recurrent fevers, a patchy or urticaria-like rash, and episodes lasting several days to a week
Common features include arthralgia or arthritis, gastrointestinal symptoms, and sicca-like complaints
Attacks are recurrent rather than continuous, with symptom-free intervals between episodes
Diagnosis is clinical with supportive NOD2 genotyping and exclusion of infection, autoimmune, and other autoinflammatory diseases
It is more frequently reported in adult women of European ancestry
Management uses anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory therapy, with variable response; some patients benefit from interleukin-1 or interleukin-6 directed treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Yao syndrome is linked to variants in NOD2, an intracellular sensor of bacterial cell-wall components that regulates inflammatory signalling. Unlike the specific NOD2 mutations causing Blau syndrome, the variants in Yao syndrome are thought to dysregulate innate immune signalling and cytokine production, producing periodic systemic inflammation. This drives recurrent fevers, dermatitis, arthralgia, and gastrointestinal symptoms without the granulomatous triad of Blau syndrome. The condition is regarded as a polygenically influenced autoinflammatory disease rather than a simple single-gene disorder, which contributes to its variable presentation and treatment response.
additionalDifferentials: Familial Mediterranean fever and other hereditary periodic fevers
additionalInvestigations: Acute-phase reactants during and between episodes
Autoantibody and infection screens to exclude alternative diagnoses
Skin biopsy of the rash where diagnosis is unclear
Gastrointestinal evaluation if bowel symptoms predominate
Assessment for sicca symptoms and salivary gland involvement
redFlags: Persistent rather than episodic inflammation suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Features of inflammatory bowel disease requiring separate evaluation
Development of amyloidosis from chronic uncontrolled inflammation
Systemic features raising concern for malignancy or infection
reference.prognosis: Yao syndrome typically follows a relapsing course with good overall life expectancy; symptoms can often be controlled with anti-inflammatory therapy, though responses vary and some patients have persistent troublesome attacks.
pitfalls: Equating any NOD2 variant with Blau syndrome or Crohn disease
Diagnosing on genotype alone without a compatible clinical picture and exclusion of mimics
Missing the episodic nature by assessing patients only during quiescent intervals
Overlooking treatable alternative causes of periodic fever
management: Control acute flares with short courses of glucocorticoids to suppress the systemic inflammation
Use maintenance anti-inflammatory therapy such as colchicine or sulfasalazine to reduce attack frequency
Escalate refractory disease to biologic therapy, particularly interleukin-1 inhibition with anakinra or canakinumab, and consider interleukin-6 blockade
Manage arthralgia or arthritis and the gastrointestinal and sicca-like symptoms symptomatically
Exclude infection, autoimmune and other autoinflammatory diseases before and during treatment, supporting the diagnosis with NOD2 genotyping
Monitor acute-phase reactants during and between episodes to gauge disease activity and treatment response
Coordinate care between rheumatology and clinical immunology for this relapsing condition
